The '''1946–47 season''' was the 48th completed season of [[The Football League]], and the first after the [[Second World War]].

This season was the first to feature a full football programme since the [[1938–39 Football League|1938–39 campaign]]. Division placings were the same as in the unfinished [[1939–40 Football League]].

==Final division tables==
Beginning with the season 1894–95, clubs finishing level on points were separated according to goal average (goals scored divided by goals conceded), or more properly put, goal ratio. In case one or more teams had the same goal difference, this system favoured those teams who had scored fewer goals. The goal average system was eventually scrapped beginning with the 1976–77 season.<ref name="rsssf">{{cite web |url=https://www.rsssf.org/engpaul/FLA/1946-47.html |title=England 1946–47 |publisher=Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation|access-date=2010-02-24}}</ref>

From the 1922–23 season, the bottom two teams of both Third Division North and Third Division South were required to apply for [[re-election (Football League)|re-election]].<ref name="Rothmans">Ian Laschke: ''Rothmans Book of Football League Records 1888–89 to 1978–79''. Macdonald and Jane’s, London & Sydney, 1980.</ref>

After a tight title race involving several clubs in the First Division, [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]] won their fifth league title, finishing one point ahead of their nearest rivals [[Manchester United F.C.|Manchester United]] (who won two league titles before the [[World War I]]) and [[Wolverhampton Wanderers]] (who had yet to win a First Division title). [[Stoke City F.C.|Stoke City]] and [[Blackpool F.C.|Blackpool]] completed the top five.

[[Leeds United F.C.|Leeds United]] were relegated in bottom place after just six wins all season. They were joined by a [[Brentford F.C.|Brentford]] side who failed to match their promising pre-war form, and would not return to the top flight until [[2021-22 Premier League|2021]].
